RESEARCH LETTER

Population-based screening cohort study reveals no association between monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), smoldering multiple myeloma (SMM), multiple myeloma (MM), and alopecia

Divija Sharma1 · Benjamin Ungar1 · Jonas A. Adalsteinsson1 · Jon Kristinn Sigurdsson2 · Kelley Sharp3 · Sigrún Thorsteinsdóttir2,10 · Saemundur Rögnvaldsson2,4 · Ásdís R Þórðardóttir2 · Brynjar Viðarsson4 · Páll T Önundarson4 · Bjarni A Agnarssond4 · Margrét Sigurðardóttird4 · Ingunn Þorsteinsdóttir4 · Ísleifur Ólafsson4 · Elías Eyþórsson4 · Ásbjörn Jónsson5 · Andri Ólafsson2 · Gauti Kjartan Gíslason2 · Ola Landgren6 · Malin Hulcrantz7 · Brian GM Durie8 · Stephen Harding9 · Thorvardur Jon Love2,4 · Sigurdur Yngvi Kristinsson2,4

Received: 12 July 2024 / Revised: 15 July 2024 / Accepted: 3 September 2024 / Published online: 14 September 2024 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2024

Keywords Multiple myeloma (MM), smoldering multiple myeloma (SMM), monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), alopecia · Nonscarring hair loss · Hair loss · Inflammatory hair loss

Alopecia in the context of hematological disorders remains incompletely characterized, particularly regarding plasma cell dyscrasias (PCDs) such as multiple myeloma (MM) and its precursors, smoldering multiple myeloma (SMM) and monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS). MGUS is characterized by abnormal monoclonal protein in the blood and stands as a precursor to more severe PCDs. Although MGUS is often asymptomatic, it carries the risk of progressing to MM. SMM, a stage between MGUS and MM, represents a more advanced stage of PCD with higher levels of monoclonal protein and plasma cells in the bone marrow. MGUS and SMM have been associated with cutaneous disorders, including alopecia, periorbital and facial purpura, petechia, scattered ecchymoses, nodules, and scleroderma-like changes of the skin; this phenomenon is termed monoclonal gammopathy of cutaneous significance (MGCS) [3]. Our study aims to explore the relationship between MGUS and subsequent PCDs and alopecia, utilizing the iStopMM database and the Icelandic Healthcare Registries system.

This cohort was drawn from the iStopMM study, a nationwide screening study for MGUS [4]. Alopecia diagnoses included alopecia areata (AA) (L63), scarring alopecia (L66, L661, L662, L663), androgenetic alopecia (AGA) (L64, L65), and telogen effluvium (L650). Since MGUS is generally an asymptomatic condition and the timing of onset prior to iStopMM screening is unknown, we included diagnoses of alopecia both before and after the identification of MGUS. We identified 3,664 individuals with MGUS, SMM, and MM and 71,159 individuals without MGUS (Table 1). No statistically significant associations were identified between MGUS and subsequent PCDs and AA, scarring alopecia, AGA, and telogen effluvium (OR:1.38 95% p = 0.28); (OR: 0.57 p = 0.21); (OR: 0.87 p = 0.77); and (OR: 1.51E-07 p = 0.93), respectively (Table 1). A sensitivity analysis was conducted where patients who eventually progressed from MGUS to SMM or MM were censored, and no significant associations were found (Table 2).

This study, utilizing the iStopMM dataset, the largest population-based screening MGUS dataset in the world, marks the first investigation into the relationship between MGUS and alopecia. The major strength lies in the comprehensive cohort where MGUS was detected by routine screening, minimizing ascertainment bias present in other studies.

The exploration between alopecia and PCDs stems from historical associations of MGUS with autoimmune conditions. A recent comprehensive study utilizing the iStopMM dataset has challenged this theory, suggesting that the previously observed association of MGUS and autoimmunity is due to bias in prior studies [5]. Limitations of this study include potential misclassification due to ICD-10 codes and possible underpowered sample sizes to detect associations. Lastly, the generalizability of these findings is needed in other populations given the ethnic homogeneity in Iceland. In summary, this nationwide screening investigation into the

relationship between PCDs and alopecia revealed no significant associations in contrast to prior literature.
